Memory is necessary, because without it nothing holds together. Yet memory also traps. It leaves people going through the motions, repeating what was once fresh until it becomes a chore. Then the practice is no longer happening in the present; it is being carried by the echo of the past. So the trouble is not ritual itself, but ritual without discovery, without immediacy, without actually entering the spirit of what it was for.
What does it mean to rely on "other power" instead of self-effort in Pure Land Buddhism?

It means recognizing that the more you try to save yourself by your own virtue, the more you may simply be strengthening the very self that wants to be saved. "Other power" is the admission that liberation does not come from ego straining to improve itself. In Pure Land language this is represented by Amida: a grace, a compassion, a power not manufactured by your own will. At first this seems to mean something outside you altogether. But more deeply, it points to that whole side of your existence that happens by itself: your life, your breath, your heart, the given character of being. Relying on other power is letting go of the claim that the separate self is the author of awakening.
How can both intense discipline and complete non-effort lead to the same spiritual problem?

Because both can become traps for the self. If you pursue intense discipline, you may become proud of your effort, your renunciation, your spiritual seriousness. The self survives by turning practice into an achievement. But if you go to the opposite extreme and insist on no effort at all, you run into the same bind. You begin asking, "Am I really doing nothing?" Even trying not to try becomes a subtle form of effort. So both paths reveal the same paradox: the one who is trying to get free is itself the difficulty. Whether you strain or refuse to strain, you eventually discover that self and other, doing and happening, are not as separate as they first seemed.
Do I have to believe in a personal father-like God to be religious?

No. Rejecting the paternal image of God does not necessarily make one an atheist. The difficulty is that people easily confuse the intelligence or ground behind the universe with a magnified authoritarian father, a beneficent tyrant with rules and punishments. That image may be emotionally powerful, but it is still an image. A genuinely religious attitude can exist without fastening on any specific picture at all. It is a relationship with the ground of your being that is not embodied in a father figure, or any other figure. In that sense, religion is less a matter of obedience to a cosmic authority and more a matter of trust—ceasing to cling to idols of the mind and allowing the unknown reality beyond all concepts to be what it is.
Why use dark or frightening images like Kali to think about ultimate reality?

Because they break the spell of our habitual assumptions. We are so used to imagining the ultimate as light, goodness, fatherhood, and reassurance that we forget life also depends on darkness, emptiness, death, and the negative principle. Kali is useful not as a final definition, but as a shock to the imagination. She reminds us that what we call good is always known against the background of what must not happen, and that death and dissolution are inseparable from rebirth and life. The dark, the void, the terrible feminine, even the blankness we fear, are not merely enemies of meaning. They are necessary counterparts. Such imagery loosens the mind from its ruts and points beyond all comforting idols toward what cannot be pictured at all.
What does it mean to relate to the ground of being without clinging to any image of God?

It means giving up the need to hold onto a mental picture, doctrine, or authority figure as if that were ultimate reality itself. Images of God often become something to grasp, and that grasping is a form of distrust. To relate to the ground of being without an image is to live in faith as letting go: not trying to capture the mystery in concepts, not chasing it, not turning it into an object outside yourself. The ground is beyond father and mother, light and darkness, life and death. You cannot get hold of it, just as you cannot turn around and see the source of your own seeing. When grasping stops, there is a discovery that this unknown foundation is not separate from you—though not the image or opinion you usually call yourself.
Why does thinking too much about the future create anxiety?

Because the same power that lets us predict also makes us painfully aware of endings. Human beings can look at the past, project patterns forward, and use that for survival. That is useful, but it comes with a price. Once you are living by anticipation, you also know that no plan finally wins, because everything comes apart in the end, whether sooner or later. So the mind becomes divided against itself: trying to secure life while knowing it cannot be secured permanently. That is why too much concern with the future turns into worry. We gained a remarkable ability through time-awareness, but we also became capable of frightening ourselves with it.
What does it mean to say that existence is musical rather than serious?

It means life is not best understood as a grim project with a final payoff, but as a pattern of movement to be participated in while it is happening. Music has rhythm, variation, style, and play. It is not there to get somewhere else; its meaning is in the playing itself. In that sense, existence is like dancing, singing, or the many games of nature, each doing its own thing in its own rhythm. Creatures, cities, days and nights all move in recurring patterns, like phrases in music. To call existence musical is to see it as playful and expressive rather than heavy with ultimate seriousness. The point is not to force it into a conclusion, but to join its swing.
How do people frustrate themselves by treating life like a task instead of a dance?

They miss what is happening by always turning it into something to get through. Instead of singing while the music is being played, they hold back because they are preoccupied with what must be achieved, completed, or secured. In that way, life becomes a burden of constant doing, and the person becomes an organism for self-frustration. The trouble is not action itself, but the refusal to let the rhythm happen. When everything is treated as a means to some later result, the present is sacrificed. But what people naturally do when they are not being pushed around is move rhythmically: they dance, sing, play, listen, swing. So the frustration comes from resisting the playful character of life and trying to make it into a duty.
